clause: 4
4.3 Charpy V-notch impact test
Standard Charpy V-notch test specimens shall be prepared and tested as specified in DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.2 Ch.1
Sec.3.
The test specimens shall be cut with their longitudinal axis transverse to the weld length, with the notch
perpendicular to the surface of the plate and positioned as follows:
— for deposited metal and butt weld test assemblies with multi-run technique, the test specimens shall be
cut at mid thickness of the weld
— for two-run welded test assemblies the specimens shall be cut on the 2nd run side, 2 mm below the
surface
— for electroslag or electrogas welded test assemblies the specimens shall be cut 2 mm below the surface
and for test piece thicknesses above 20 mm additional test specimens shall be cut 2 mm below the root
side of the test assembly
— for one-side automatic welding processes, the test specimens shall be cut 2 mm below the face side and 2
mm below the root side of the test assembly.
The average absorbed energy value shall comply with the requirements of the applicable subsequent section.
One individual value may be less than the required average value provided that it is not less than 70% of this
value.

3 Testing procedure
The test welds shall normally be made on the materials listed in the rules DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.2 Ch.2 for which
approval of the welding consumable is desired. Any grade of structural steel (see DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.2 Ch.2
Sec.2) may be used for the preparation of the all-weld-metal test assemblies.
The test specimens shall be made under controlled conditions, on metal deposited from the filler metal in
question.
When a test weld is performed, the edges of the plates shall be bevelled either by mechanical machining or
by oxygen cutting, in the latter case, a descaling of the edges is necessary.
After being welded, the test assemblies shall not be subjected to any heat treatment.
If manufacturer request approval for the heat-treated condition, additional test pieces shall be prepared and
heat-treated accordingly.
It is recommended that the welded assembly is subjected to radiographic examination to ascertain whether
there are any defects in the weld prior to testing.

gold_answer:
- 서비스 공급자는 보호 외함, 인터페이스 및 컨버터, UPS, 음향 비콘, 해제 장치, 마이크로폰, 알람/운영 패널의 상태를 포함한 점검 절차와 체크리스트를 보유해야 합니다.
- 최종 기록 매체에 기록된 모든 데이터의 가용성 및 제조사의 유지관리 계획에 따른 특별 항목이 포함되어야 합니다.
- 2014년 7월 1일 이후 설치된 장치의 경우, 성능 테스트 기능과 ECDIS 디스플레이, AIS, 롤링 모션, 구성 데이터 및 전자 항해 일지(장착 시)가 포함된 최종 기록 매체의 데이터가 포함되어야 합니다.

clause: 1
1.2.9 Reporting
The UTM report shall be made in the Society's electronic reporting format, Pegasus, available at
www.dnv.com, and uploaded as hcz-file to DNV online tool Veracity.
Prior to commencing measurements on board, in addition to the measured values, the original scantlings, the
minimum thickness and the substantial corrosion limits shall be stored in the electronic report.
When on board, measured thicknesses shall be continuously recorded in the Society’s electronic report form,
based on the operator’s working notes, photos and sketches and are regularly to be made available for the
Society's review and verification.
Upon completion of the measurements on board the operator shall provide the Society with a temporary
electronic draft of the results presented in the Society's electronic report form, and supplied with the
operator’s notes, as found necessary. The location of the measurements shall be illustrated by sketches or
drawings.
The preliminary report shall include a longitudinal strength evaluation when required, (IMO Res.A.744(18)
Annex 12) valid for oil tanker with length above 130 meters and over 10 years of age, e.g. at the third
renewal survey and subsequent renewal surveys.
Final reporting in original electronic form and in a non-editable electronic form (e.g. PDF-format) shall be
presented to the Society within two (2) weeks after the job is terminated. The firm shall have the Society’s
verification of each separate job, documented in the report by the Society's signature and the text 'Verified
and evaluated'.
The report shall include a copy of the certificate of approval of the firm.

(manufacturer/DNV)
— prepare and submit final approval report including all required documentation and test results reports

gold_answer:
- 운영자는 소음 및 진동 분야, 측정 장비 취급에 대한 지식을 보유해야 하며, ISO 18436-2에 따른 최소 Category I 인증을 보유하는 것이 권장됩니다.

question: 선체 내부에서 수행하는 검사 시, 내측 접근이 불가능하여 추가 문서나 외부 조사가 필요한 항목에는 어떤 것들이 있는가?

clause: 4
4.2 Areas where additional documentation or survey from outside is
required
When inspection is carried out from the inside of the hull, additional documentation may be required
to document appendages and equipment which is not accessible from the inside. These items shall be
documented to have a sufficient low risk without being inspected. If that documentation is missing or
incomplete ROV or diving inspection may be required. Examples of areas where this may be required are:
— bilge keels and moonpools (for ship shaped units)
— fairlead foundations
— anchor rack to hull
— condition of sacrificial anodes if used for corrosion protection of the hull.
It may also be required to inspect sea water inlets and sea chests if units are not prepared for inspection
from the inside.
Other areas which are not easily covered by inspection from the inside are e.g. coating breakdown and
localized corrosion.
Performing alternating bottom surveys from inside and outside may be a viable approach to establish
sufficient documentation of the full scope of the bottom survey.
Documentation including calculations and logs from planned maintenance programmes related to equipment
and items listed above which can be documented to have low risk or long service life may be accepted for the
purpose of crediting the bottom survey.

clause: 1
1.1 Introduction
Following a large number of requests from yards and designers on clarification of the calculation principles for
liquid equalization resulting from applying the SOLAS 2009 damage stability regulations DNV has compiled a
number of guidance notes on cross-flooding.
It will be recalled that the first version of IMO's standard method was adopted as early as in 1973 for use
with the probabilistic equivalent to SOLAS 1960 as well as the deterministic requirements of SOLAS 1960 and
its subsequent amendments. The increased focus on cross-flooding in the 2009 revision of SOLAS 1974 made
it necessary to update the recommendations, which were published as IMO Res. MSC.245(83) in 2007. After
the entry into force of the revised SOLAS Ch.II-1, international experience with the new regulations showed
that the recommendations needed further updates and corrections. These were in turn adopted as IMO Res.
MSC.362(92) in 2013.
The official interpretation to SOLAS Ch.II-1 Reg.7-2.2 allowing intermediate stages of flooding to be
disregarded as instantaneous, if fluid equalization is achieved in 60 s or less, has been a source of
frequent discussions. The complexity of practical design solutions and the widespread desire to utilise this
simplification was never foreseen when the IMO resolution was drafted. In particular, the use of high-capacity
duct solutions has proven important. DNV has also noted that constructs deviating from what is described in
the resolution can be a source of misunderstandings of the hydraulic principles.
The two most prominent issues raised are:
— cross-flooding by structural ducts
— calculation of pressure loss due to air pipes.

2.1.5 Test plan
Prior to commencing testing, a test plan shall be submitted to the Society for review against applicable
requirements of the selected in-water cleaning standard. The test plan shall be prepared by the testing
organization based input from the cleaning company, including applicable specifications and/or limitations for
cleaning and capturing. The test plan shall describe:
— the scope of testing
— the selected target areas for cleaning
— the areas selected for assessing the efficiency of removing micro- and/or macrofouling, these areas are
a subset of the selected target areas for cleaning and shall be selected to be representative for the whole
target area for cleaning
— the methods applied for sampling and analysis
— the standard operating procedures (SOP) and the quality system applied by the testing organization.
The test plan shall specify how representative samples are taken. Careful considerations should be given by
the testing organization, that the selected sampling locations and the sampling process do not significantly
impact the cleaning operations.
For testing of the efficiency of removing micro- and/or macrofouling, the test plan shall describe the
methodology applied for randomly selecting representative areas used for testing and for objectively
evaluating levels of micro- and/or macrofouling prior to and after cleaning.
The test plan shall contain relevant environmental, health, and safety plans to ensure that samples are taken
in a safe manner and collected debris is disposed suitably.

gold_evidence.context:
clause: 2
2.5 Progressive couplings
The term progressive is used for couplings which have stiffness significantly increasing with the applied
torque.
For progressive couplings the parameters (mean torque, vibratory torque, frequency, temperature,
permanent set) are considered to be interdependent. Of this reason the testing shall be more extensive than
for linear couplings. Simplifications may be used, but this may cause restrictions in the application field of the
couplings.
In principle the 4 first test conditions mentioned for linear couplings
(f, Tm/TKN, Tv/TKN, temperature) shall be fully intersected, i.e. all combinations of conditions apply. However,
a reduced amount of combinations with frequency and temperature may be accepted without resulting in
restricted applications. The mean torques and vibratory torques shall be tested in all applicable combinations.
For couplings designed so that a permanent set is likely to occur and to alter the dynamic properties
significantly, the tests with different combinations of mean and vibratory torques shall be repeated with the
max permissible permanent set (i.e. when the elements have to be replaced).
Further, all required testing for linear couplings also apply for progressive.

clause: 2
2.3 Extent of testing
The extent of the testing shall be sufficient for evaluation of the following:
1)
Dynamic stiffness (K) and relative damping (ψ) as functions of:
— Frequency (f)
— Mean torque (Tm)
— Vibratory torque (Tv)
— Internal temperature (θ)
— Permanent set (for progressive couplings).
For conformal designs this may be shown in non-dimensional graphs by relating the torques to the
nominal coupling torque (TKN).
2)
Permissible power loss capability (PkV ) as function of:
— Coupling size (or TKN)
— Ambient temperature.
3)
Permissible vibratory torque verification regarding fatigue, by combination of steps of mean torque and
superimposed vibratory load.
Depending on the specified level of the permissible vibratory torque (independent of limitations on heat
dissipation due to damping) a verification of fatigue values may be required. If required, a coupling element
shall be cyclically loaded with twice the permissible vibratory torque for 106 cycles and with a frequency
sufficiently low to prevent excessive rubber temperatures. Prior to dynamic testing, the elements shall be
tested in accordance with the agreed production testing, i.e. normally a “quasi-static” twisting.

1 General
There are some areas where there are prescriptive requirements from the competent authority (HSE) or
items which are considered good practice, and are therefore expected to be complied with. The list below
includes some of those items. Note, this list is not exhaustive and reference should be made to the current
legislation.
Lifeboat capacity
PFEER Reg.15 ACOP require that the lifeboat capacity onboard for 150% of the POB (personnel onboard),
unless and alternative standard is justified or called for on the basis of the PFEER assessment
Grab bags
PFEER Reg.18 ACOP requires that there are provided for each person a smoke hood, heat resistant gloves
and a source of light.
In practice these are often grouped into a grab bag (where the heli-transit-suit is also stored) so that in case
of an emergency you take one item with you. However, there is no requirement to put them in a grab bag.
Emergency signals
PFEER Reg.11 (2) includes specific details on the alarm signals. These are not the same as International
Maritime Rules and Guidance, and need to be followed. Few exemptions are given from these prescriptive
requirements.
Temporary refuge (TR) SCR 2005 and SCR 2015
Temporary refuge is designed to provide a place where the personnel can safety muster and stay until such
time as the OIM makes a decision about any incident and the need for abandonment. The TR shall therefore
provide:
— a safe place for muster
— command and control facilities
— communications
— medical facilities
— access to the means of escape and evacuation
— breathable atmosphere for the POB for the duration that the TR is intended to be needed.

at LBP/2, or at the load line mark position. Checking only the equivalent draught (i.e. at LCF) is not
acceptable.
The loading computer shall check the maximum draught, and give a warning if the draught is exceeded. The
loading computer may also check the draught limits for the seasonal load line marks (winter, summer, fresh
water, tropical, tropical fresh). If this is an option, there should normally be an input for the 'season' for the
specific loading condition, so that the correct mark/draught is selected. For special consideration for timber
load line, see [6.6]. The same also applies for other special marks on the ship side, like ICE (maximum
draught in ice infested water) or other condition based draught limitation (mode of vessel, reduced number
of passenger).
For vessels with permanent thrusters or skegs below the normal base line draught, the draught at the lowest
part of these shall also be displayed.
For vessels equipped with retractable appendages such as thrusters or sonars, there should be a function
for displaying the draught at these when applied in their deepest position. For this function, it is proposed to
discuss with the owners on how this function shall work and be displayed.

2.1 Principles
Prior to fatigue testing, the crankshaft shall be tested as required by quality control procedures, e.g. for
chemical composition, mechanical properties, surface hardness, hardness depth and extension, fillet surface
finish, etc.
The test samples should be prepared so as to represent the lower end of the acceptance range, e.g. for
induction hardened crankshafts this means the lower range of acceptable hardness depth, the shortest
extension through a fillet, etc. Otherwise the mean value test results should be corrected with a confidence
interval: a 90% confidence interval may be used both for the sample mean and the standard deviation.
The test results, when applied in Sec.2, shall be evaluated to represent the mean fatigue strength, with or
without taking into consideration the 90% confidence interval as mentioned above. The standard deviation
should be considered by taking the 90% confidence into account. Subsequently the result to be used as the
fatigue strength is then the mean fatigue strength minus one standard deviation.
If the evaluation aims to find a relationship between (static) mechanical properties and the fatigue strength,
the relation shall be based on the real (measured) mechanical properties, not on the specified minimum
properties.
The calculation technique presented in [2.4] was developed for the original staircase method. However, since
there is no similar method dedicated to the modified staircase method the same is applied for both.
Normally, small specimen tests shall be done with tensile load. The shear (torsion) fatigue strength can
then be found by using the equivalent stress (von Mises) approach (observing the restriction for cgf forging
mentioned in [3.5]).

2 Qualification and approval of procedures for robotic welding -
joining and overlay/clad welding
DNV rules and offshore standards, and other relevant international standards for welding procedures
qualification require that a change from manual (or semi-automatic) to fully mechanized (or fully automatic)
welding process shall be re-qualified, see DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.2 Ch.4 Sec.5 and DNV-OS-C401.
The process for qualification and approval of robotic welding procedures is similar to that described in DNV-
CG-0287 Hybrid laser-arc welding.
The qualification consists of the following main steps, as illustrated in Figure 1:
1)
Defining the essential process parameters and tolerance ranges.
This would typically be established through systematic trials using different welding parameters, and
result in target parameters for the process, including process parameter ranges giving acceptable
results. It is recommended to use multi-dimensional statistical modelling which has proven to be a
powerful tool to handle this task.
2)
Implementing the results into practical welding.
A stable and repeatable welding process shall be achieved. When a novel welding process is introduced
in a workshop, there is by experience always a 'trial and error phase' before the process becomes stable
and repeatable. Formal class approval work should not start in this turbulent phase, but wait until the
process is under control, and can be demonstrated to be stable and repeatable.
3)
Approval, comprising establishment of a pWPS, WPQT, WPQR and WPS.
This step follows the same strategy as described in the Society's rules for conventional welding
processes.

Pressure transducers shall be mounted to measure the fluid pressures inside the tank. The sensing area
should be positioned flush with the inner tank wall.
The shock resistance of pressure sensors should be sufficient not to interfere with the impacts and

3.3 Wear testing procedure
The wear test shall be performed in accordance with ASTM G77, with the following data:
— Material of the shaft used in the test and its properties are to be specified and shall be equivalent to the
typical mating material, e.g. alloyed steel or stainless steel or copper alloy.
— Diameter of the shaft: the shaft diameter depends on the bearing size. The running clearance should be
considered in the wear test
— Motion of the shaft: continuous rotation.
— Circumferential velocity should be 6 m/s for oil or water lubrication and should be 3 m/s for grease
lubrication.
— Lubrication: sea water or substitute ocean water (23°C ±2°C), or mineral oil (80°C ±2°C), or grease
(80°C ±2°C) according to the applicable lubrication type.
— Surface roughness of the test shaft: Ra shall not exceed 0.5 μm for stainless steel and Ra shall not exceed

0.8 μm for copper alloy.
— Interface pressure: maximum nominal surface pressure ±10%.
— Duration of the test: until the coefficient of friction and wear rate remains constant (at least 192 h). The
wear of bushings shall be measured either continuously or regularly. If measured regularly, the wear shall
be measured by disassembling every 48 h until a constant wear rate has been achieved (minimum of four
points of measurements).
The parameters shall be recorded:
— dimensions of the test specimen
— wear vs. time
— coefficient of friction vs. time
— temperature of the test specimen during the test cycle
— deviation of load from the maximum nominal surface pressure.

clause: 4
4.3.2 Design accelerations
The design accelerations used for dimensioning of tanks and supports are given in DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.5 Ch.7
Sec.4 [6.1.2]. These formulas are considered to give conservative design accelerations for traditional type
C gas carriers. Alternatively, for standard gas carriers, the envelope accelerations as given in DNV-RU-SHIP
Pt.3 Ch.4 Sec.3 [3.3] may be used for the design of the tanks. A margin on the design values should be
considered to account for uncertainty in preliminary data during early design phase.
Note that the design accelerations may also be determined by direct calculations and used in connection
with the acceleration ellipse, but this has not been the general practice for past and current designs. This is
mainly because the dynamic contribution on the scantling is normally significantly less compared to the static
contribution, and an optimization with regard to the dynamic pressure has not been considered necessary.
If direct calculations are carried out (i.e. a wave load analysis) to determine the accelerations, the following
assumptions should be made for ULS design:
— Ship speed of 5 knots.
— A known wave spectrum with short crested waves based on North Atlantic wave environment to be used.
— All headings considered equally probable and the average load values over all headings shall be applied.
— Loads shall be taken at probability level of 10-8. This corresponds to the most probable largest load the
ship will experience during 108 wave encounters in the North Atlantic and is normally interpreted as being
equivalent to a service life of 25 years.

The objective of this class programme (CP) is to describe the type approval (TA) scheme for cable ties.

clause: 1
1.2 Scope
This CP gives a description of the procedures and requirements related to documentation, design and type
testing applicable for TA of cable ties.
This CP does not set the design requirements to the cable ties. TA is based on compliance with design
requirements given in the rules and/or other regulations and standards. The CP describes the applicable
design requirements and how to document compliance with the requirements in order to obtain a TA
certificate for the equipment. This includes, where relevant, technical requirements for how the type tests

clause: 2
2.4 Impact testing
The following is required:
— Impact tests on Charpy V-notch specimens shall be made for:
— All steel grades without specified impact toughness requirements: for products with wall thickness ≥
10 mm.
— All steel grades with specified impact toughness requirements and grades for sub-zero service
temperature: for products with wall thickness ≥ 6 mm.
— all steel grades which must comply with the requirements provided in DNV-RU-SHIP Pt.5 Ch.7 for
products with wall thickness ≥ 3 mm.
— Transverse impact specimens shall be used when outside diameter ≥ 200 mm, longitudinal specimens
may be used for outside diameter is < 200 mm.
— For sub-size specimens, the width of the specimen shall be 7.5 mm, 5 mm, or 2.5 mm, whichever is
larger and possible to prepare, and the actual measured energy shall be reported (without conversion to
normal specimen).
— at least three sets of Charpy V-notch specimens shall be tested.
— Tests shall be tested at temperatures +20°C, 0°C, –20°C, and lower temperatures when required by the
applicable standard.
— For approval of ‘grades for low temperature applications’, tests shall be carried out at the lowermost
temperature for which approval is requested (will be specified on approval certificate).
— The impact toughness requirements shall fulfil the corresponding DNV rule requirements at and above the
specified test temperature. Grades without specified impact toughness requirements shall obtain minimum
27 J at +20°C, unless otherwise agreed.

question: 와이어 인발용 바(bar)에 사용되는 강재의 결정립 크기 요건과 미세 결정립(fine grain)으로 인정받기 위한 알루미늄(Al), 니오븀(Nb), 바나듐(V) 등의 함량 조건은 무엇인가요?
gold_answer:
- 와이어 인발용 강재의 오스테나이트 결정립 크기는 ASTM E112에 따라 5 이하(5 or finer)여야 한다.
- 알루미늄 단독 사용 시 최소 함량은 0.020% 이상이거나 Al 대 N 비율이 2:1 이상이어야 한다.
- 알루미늄과 니오븀 혼합 사용 시 알루미늄 최소 0.015%, 니오븀 최소 0.010%를 포함해야 하며, 알루미늄과 바나듐 혼합 사용 시 알루미늄 최소 0.015%, 바나듐 최소 0.030%를 포함해야 한다.

clause: 6
6.2.4 Extent of testing
The extent of the testing shall be sufficient for evaluation of the following:
Dynamic stiffness (K) in compression and/or shear and relative damping ( ψ ) as functions of:
— frequency (f)
— mean load (Fm) vibratory load (FV)
— temperature (θ) (optional)
— permanent set.
For various element sizes of similar designs this may be shown in non-dimensional graphs by relating the
loads to the permissible element load.
Prior to dynamic testing, the elements shall be tested in accordance with the agreed production testing.
It is normally acceptable to assume that the functions of the parameters mean load, vibratory load and
frequency are not interdependent, but form discrete dependencies. This means that following set up may
apply:
K = Kref · f(f) · f(Fm) · f(FV)

Figure 1 Load vs displacement diagram
The load-displacement diagram for elements with high damping occurs as a combination of an ellipse and a
parallelogram. The stiffness is evaluated as the slope of a (dotted) line drawn through midpoints between the
ascending and the descending paths for all displacement positions except near the ends where there might
be some deviation from a straight line.
The damping is evaluated as relative damping
ψ = area of hysteresis loop/elastic work (hatched area).
When other methods are used, e.g. such as evaluating stiffness as the ratio between the load at max.
displacement and the max. displacement respectively, evaluating damping by means of tan ε (phase angle
between peak load and load at max. displacement), it is assumed that the damping properties are fully
viscous. Since this assumption rarely holds, the results shall be handled with care. For use in vibration
analysis these elements will be considered to have a wider deviation than other elements.

gold_evidence.context:
Background
2
The report of the forty-seventh meeting of the GESAMP-Ballast Water Working Group
(GESAMP-BWWG) (MEPC 84/4/3) mentions in paragraph 3.2 that the Group initiated
discussions on topics listed in the agenda for its tenth stocktaking workshop. Time constraints
did not allow the Group to discuss all matters at the stocktaking workshop in detail, and it
agreed to revisit them at a future opportunity and submit its report to a future session. Given
this reality, and in order to contribute to the stocktaking exercise and the need for continued
research and monitoring of present and future ballast water management and impacts, this
document summarizes a recent report1 on ballast water operations, discharges and their
impacts in the Gulf of California (GoC) from future liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker traffic.
The majority of the findings in the report are based on a comprehensive review of scientific
literature. Modelling methodologies are summarized.

Report background
3
Increased LNG tanker traffic in the GoC introduces stressors like underwater radiated
noise (URN) and the risk of whale strikes, while invasive aquatic species can outcompete
native species, disrupt food webs, introduce pathogens, and alter habitats. Collectively, these
changes have the potential to adversely affect the marine environment, native and migratory
species, and nearby coastal communities through both direct and cumulative impacts.
4
Invasive
aquatic
species
impose
a
global
economic
cost
estimated
at 345 billion $USD/5.9 trillion MXN, with North America bearing nearly half (48%) of reported
invasion costs.2,3 From 1992 to 2019, aquatic and semi-aquatic invasive species cost Mexico
an estimated 4.16 billion USD/78.65 billion MXN, representing 78% of the total economic
damages caused by invasive species in the country during that period.4 Preventing introduction
is the most cost-effective strategy; once a species establishes and spreads, eradication
becomes nearly impossible and exponentially more expensive.
5
LNG tankers can operate on "single-stop" voyages, meaning they arrive at export
terminals effectively empty of cargo and thus under full ballast volumes to maintain stability.
The Saguaro LNG Phase 3 project is projected to involve the discharge of up to 30 million
metric tonnes (30 billion litres) of ballast water from tankers annually, if LNG tankers discharge
at each port call.

From a climate change and regulatory perspective, the biogenic CO2 from liquefied
biomethane (LBM) combustion is afforded an emissions credit. As such attention is applied to
methane slip. Though for the purposes of this submission methane slip of 3.5% was used,

approved by the Committee and should be resubmitted in accordance with the methodology
developed by GESAMP-LCA WG. Further industry and literature evidence on methane slip is
needed before a representative value and subsequently a "representative and conservative"
TtW default emission factor for methane-based pathways value can be determined.

proponent took a step towards establishing representative value. The use of factory
acceptance test (FAT) data establishes a range and offers a framework for future refinement
as additional primary data and literature values can be incorporated. To achieve
conservativeness, a systematic adjustment process was implemented, specifically designed
to account for uncertainty while maintaining alignment with policy objectives and the

gold_evidence.file_name: MEPC 84-INF.19 - Information on the amended type approval of the inTank BWTSballast water management system (Norway).pdf
gold_evidence.context:
Executive summary
8
The type approval for the inTank BWTS has been amended to also include an
alternate TRO sensor and models inTank FITT BWTS and inTank SuperFITT BWTS.
Description of the BWMS
9
The inTank BWTS has two means of delivering the biocide (sodium hypochlorite) into
the ballast water, either by generating it on board through electrochlorination (EC) or by using
sodium hypochlorite stored in a bulk chemical storage tank (BC). The inTank BWTS employs
no treatment on uptake or discharge. It injects the biocide and neutralization agent directly to
the ballast water tanks while the ship is underway.
10
The required dose for the inTank BWTS is a concentration-time (CT) of ≥120 mg-h/L
TRO. A CT of 120 mg-h/L TRO is achieved using minimum holding times in the range
of 24 to 60 hours, with a corresponding average TRO dose between 5 and 2 mg/L. Before
discharge, the neutralization agent (sodium thiosulfate) is injected by in-tank circulation until
the remaining TRO concentration is below 0.1 mg/L.
11
The main components of the inTank EC BWTS are an EC (treatment) module and a
Dosing module, while other components common to both the inTank EC BWTS and the inTank
BC BWTS are the De-Chlor (neutralization) module and mixing nozzles. The EC module
generates biocide.

Modifications made to the BWMS and evaluation thereof
12
The design of the inTank BWTS has been modified to also include an alternate
amperometric TRO sensor manufactured by Halogen Systems Inc. The TRO sensor is located
on the spool piece of the Dosing module and monitors the TRO of the ballast water, as it
passes the Dosing module in the circulation loop. The dosing of chemicals is performed
downstream of the TRO sensor. DNV has monitored and surveyed shipboard functional testing
of the inTank BWTS with the Halogen TRO sensor in control, on board the barge Saipem S44
in the port of Rotterdam during 2023. In total, about 60 hours of operation, treating more
than 10,000 m3 of ballast water, were logged with appropriate readings. Also, reference
readings from the original DPD TRO sensor were recorded and compared with the alternate
amperometric TRO sensor, showing a good match. The Halogen TRO sensor and the original
DPD TRO sensor have also been compared in bench scale testing for almost 900 hours, where
results have been verified by DNV. This study showed that the Halogen TRO sensor offers a
comparable performance in BWMS applications, compared to the DPD TRO sensor. DNV has
also performed a design evaluation of the two TRO sensors, which included technology,
accuracy, calibration and maintenance. DNV was able to conclude that the alternate Halogen
TRO sensor is interchangeable with the original TRO sensor.

gold_evidence.file_name: MEPC 84-7-25 - Status on climate change and the need for regular updatesto support decision-making at IMO (Norway).pdf
gold_evidence.context:
1
Resolution A.1196(34) on the Revised Strategic Plan for the Organization for the
six-year period 2024 to 2029 was adopted on 3 December 2025. Tackling climate change is
included in the vision statement of the revised strategic plan. Further, the Strategic Plan states,
"climate change has been recognized as one of the greatest challenges of our time, a
phenomenon whose consequences have negative impacts on the planet and which can
undermine the ability of all countries to achieve sustainable development".
2
In light of the adjournment of MEPC/ES.2 and the pending adoption of the
amendments to MARPOL Annex VI, and the delay in implementation of the 2023 IMO GHG
Strategy, it is the view of Norway that awareness on the status and impacts of climate change
is important information for IMO's decision-making process. The purpose of this document is
to provide a brief update on the current status of the climate and to propose a way forward on
future updates.

4
The concentration of CO2 reached a new record level in 2024 of 423.9 ± 0.2 parts per
million (ppm) as reported by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO)4. This is an
increase of 52% compared to pre-industrial levels of ~278 ppm. The concentration increased
by 3.5 ppm from 2023 to 2024, which is larger than the mean increase over the past 10 years
of 2.57 ppm yr-1. The main driver of the change in the atmospheric abundance of CO2 is
emissions from fossil fuel burning. The emissions of CO2 from fossil fuels reached a new record
level in 2024 of 10.3 ± 0.5 Gt C yr−1 an increase of 1.1% since 2023, according to the latest
Global Carbon Budget5. The average annual growth rate in fossil CO2 emissions over the most
recent decade (2015 to 2024) is 0.8% and lower than 2.1% over the previous decade
(2005 to 2014). About half of the CO2 emitted accumulates in the atmosphere, while the rest
is taken up by the ocean and terrestrial ecosystems. The long-term rise in atmospheric CO2 is
driven by fossil fuel combustion, whereas variability in the strength of land and ocean carbon
sinks causes year-to-year variations in the CO2 growth rate. It is a concern that these sinks
may become less effective as the climate continues to warm.

This analysis shows that differences in the applied default WtT emission factors

of implementation and the scale of the resulting compliance deficits. Based on operational data
from 139 LNG carriers, the findings highlight that these effects occur within a ship type that
has limited scope to adjust fuel use or operational profiles in response to more stringent
GFI requirements. This should not be interpreted as an inability to improve performance over
time, but as an indication that short-term compliance outcomes are strongly influenced by
upstream assumptions.

The results should be interpreted in the context of the specific operational
characteristics of LNG carriers, which differ fundamentally from other ship types due to the
need to continuously manage naturally generated BOG for safety reasons. LNG carriers
predominantly rely on the efficient use of BOG as a primary energy source, particularly for the

gold_evidence.context:
clause: 2023
조문 2023절 2023. 2023. The CII framework is a regulatory measure that annually rates ships from A to E based
on their CO2 emissions per transport work, calculated using key parameters such as fuel
consumption and transport work.
2
The Committee agreed to commence a phase 2 review for a comprehensive revision
of the CII regulatory framework from 2026, using the IMO Data Collection System (IMO DCS)
data collected with enhanced granularity as analytical input for this purpose. Accordingly, from
2026, the IMO DCS will include, inter alia, the reporting of fuel consumption by consumer type
(including total and "not under way" fuel consumption), laden distance travelled on a voluntary
basis, total amount of onshore power supplied, and total transport work, which had not been
previously collected.
3
While the enhanced granularity of the IMO DCS was introduced for data collection
and analytical purposes to support future improvements to the CII regime, it has been identified
that, without clear clarification of its interaction with the current calculation framework, data
collected from 2026 onwards may lead to unintended adverse impacts on the current CII
calculation. This could potentially undermine consistency in regulatory implementation across
the global fleet.

6
However, with the inclusion of "total transport work" as a new reporting item under the
enhanced granularity of the IMO DCS from 2026, there is a risk of misinterpretation that such
data must be immediately applied in CII calculation. Such an application was neither discussed
nor agreed upon by the Committee. Rather, the collection of actual transport work data is
understood to be intended solely for the assessment of the demand-based transport work
under the CII Guidelines, G3 in support of the phase 2 review of the CII framework.
7
Furthermore, while paragraph 7.12 of the 2024 Guidelines for the development of a
Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines), as amended by
resolution MEPC.401(83), includes ship-type-specific metrics for the collection of transport
work, it is noted that further data analysis, as well as thorough consideration and agreement
by the Committee, would be required before reflecting such data in CII calculations.
8
Therefore, it is proposed that, until the phase 2 review for the comprehensive revision
of the CII framework is completed and any new metrics or calculation approaches are formally
adopted, the CII Guidelines, G1 be explicitly clarified to maintain the use of supply-based
transport work (Ws), based on DWT or GT as applicable, as a proxy consistent with the current
approach.

gold_evidence.file_name: MEPC 84-12-2 - Associated protective measures for the Reserva Nacional Dorsal de Nasca (Nasca Ridge Natio... (Peru).pdf
gold_evidence.context:
1
At its eighty-third session, MEPC approved, in principle, the designation of the
Reserva Nacional Dorsal de Nasca (Nasca Ridge National Reserve) (RNDN) as a Particularly
Sensitive Sea Area (PSSA), based on the proposal submitted by Peru (MEPC 83/12/1) and
assessed in accordance with the Revised guidelines for the identification and designation of
Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas (resolution A.982(24), as amended by resolution
MEPC.267(68)).
2
The Committee determined that the characteristics of the RNDN met the ecological,
scientific and vulnerability criteria set out in the guidelines, including its high biological value
and high sensitivity to physical, chemical and biological disturbances. It also invited Peru to
further develop the associated protective measures and to submit these to MEPC
(MEPC 83/17, paragraph 12.12).

6
Given its uniqueness, relative isolation, and associated degree of endemism,
the RNDN is particularly vulnerable. In this context, it is necessary to apply the precautionary
approach, as articulated in the Guidelines on incorporation of the precautionary approach in
the context of specific IMO activities (resolution MEPC.67(37)). These guidelines recommend
a precautionary and anticipatory approach, rather than a reactive approach, and establish that
"where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall
not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental
degradation."

However, trends identified through the collection of this data, and in particular the

Sub-Committee for consideration when further discussing the development of the
IMO database.

1
Having recalled the agreement at the seventy-third session of the Marine Environment
Protection Committee (MEPC 73) that no work with regard to the Action Plan to Address
Marine Plastic Litter from Ships would be requested of sub-committees prior to the
development of a well-defined scope of work for actions, MEPC 83 invited interested Member
States and international organizations to submit proposals for such actions. This document
responds to that invitation and outlines how the collection of data on lost or discharged fishing
gear can be progressed while discussions on the specifics of the enhanced reporting
requirements by the Sub-Committee on Pollution Prevention and Response (PPR) continue.
2
Abandoned, lost or otherwise discarded fishing gear (ALDFG) is considered one of
the most harmful forms of marine plastic litter, if not the most harmful. * Although there has
been direct harm to the marine environment observed due to fishing gear, limited analysis has
been undertaken on the scope of ALDFG currently in the marine environment. As the fishing
industry is geographically spread, with fleets that operate in all areas of waters in both national
and international waters, ALDFG can be released in open water and mobilized over large
distances, reaching sensitive habitats, feeding and fishing grounds and shipping lanes.
This can affect the marine environment, the broader economy and local industries.

- IACS Rec.165 Rev.1은 설계자, 조선소, 계산 담당 기술 관리자 및 대안과 동등성 승인에 관여하는 기타 조직을 대상으로 합니다.
- 해당 권고안은 CSR 및 기타 요구사항으로부터의 편차(deviations)가 GBS를 준수함을 입증하는 경우에도 적용됩니다.
- 선급협회(Classification Societies)가 제출된 정보의 CSR 준수 여부 또는 구조적 안전성 수준이 요구사항과 동등한지 평가할 때 적용됩니다.

gold_evidence.file_name: MSC 111-21-3 - IAPH Cyber Resilience Guidelines for Emerging Technologies (IAPH).pdf
gold_evidence.context:
Background
1
In July 2021, IAPH published its Cybersecurity Guidelines for Ports and Port Facilities.
The guidelines were brought to the attention of both the IMO Facilitation (FAL) and Maritime
Safety (MSC) Committees, and, following the MSC 104 and FAL 46 respective decisions, they
were recognized and referenced as industry standards within the Guidelines on maritime cyber
risk management (MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.2).
2
At MSC 107, the Committee agreed to establish a new output to undertake a
comprehensive review of the 2017 Guidelines on maritime cyber risk management
(MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.2) and identify possible next steps to enhance maritime cybersecurity.
This was endorsed by IAPH in document MSC 107/17/28 which further highlighted the critical
importance of cybersecurity as an inherent component of the Maritime Single Window (MSW)
and all development of digital infrastructure in ports and maritime transport. IAPH reiterated its
support to amend these guidelines by co-sponsoring document MSC 109/7/1 which proposed
to further develop cybersecurity standards for ships and port facilities to enhance
maritime cybersecurity.

3
Furthermore, in recognizing the vast opportunities and risks of operating in an
increasingly digital landscape, IAPH co-sponsored document FAL 49/8/1 proposing a way
forward for the development of an IMO strategy on maritime digitalization.
4
In light of these proposals, IAPH has developed a new set of Cyber Resilience
Guidelines containing a framework for mitigating cyber threats associated with new and
evolving technologies in the maritime industry, including key considerations, best practices,
and regulatory recommendations to ensure secure implementation of emerging technologies.
5
At MSC 110, IAPH submitted document MSC 110/7/1 containing an overview of the
Guidelines and a link to a draft version. With this submission, IAPH presents the published
version that is now available in English and Spanish.
IAPH Cyber Resilience Guidelines for Emerging Technologies in the Maritime
Supply Chain

gold_evidence.file_name: MSC 111-INF.13 - Information regarding submarine cable damage (the Nautical Institute an...).pdf
gold_evidence.context:
Introduction
1
Submarine telecommunications and power cables constitute critical global
infrastructure supporting international communications, financial systems and cross-border
electricity transmission. Their continued integrity is essential to economic stability and societal
resilience.
2
Maritime activities remain the primary external risk to submarine cables. Increasing
evidence indicates that anchors unintentionally deployed or dragged while vessels are
underway represent a significant and preventable source of damage1.
3
In addition to potential infrastructure damage, such incidents may reflect onboard
deficiencies in equipment securing, bridge awareness or operational control during passage.
4
Interactions between fishing gear and subsea cables can pose serious safety risks to
fishers and other mariners, reinforcing the need for practical prevention methods and clear
communication.

The goal of this stage is to broadly secure actual operational data and sea trial results
from ships applying the non-mandatory MASS Code. To this end, the following are proposed:

Development of standardized reporting forms: Since standardized reporting

proposed to develop standardized forms, referencing the template in the

System (GISIS) to allow Member States and international organizations to

7
Collected data should be analyzed regularly to identify technical gaps and safety
impediments. Therefore, the establishment and role of a dedicated review group are proposed
as follows:
.1
Establishment of a data review group: It is proposed to operate a dedicated
'MASS Data Review Group' in the form of a working group (WG) or
correspondence group (CG) to analyze collected data annually and report
the results to the Committee.
.2
Focus of analysis: The analysis should focus on identifying systemic risks,
technical limitations, and areas where the functional requirements of the
non-mandatory code are insufficient or impractical in actual operating
conditions.

Human element
51
Annex 2 contains the completed checklist for considering and addressing the human
element. The proposal of the Russian Federation does not lead to significant consequences
associated with the human element, and the vast majority of answers relate to the training of
seafarers in the future (the development of new training courses is possible).
Administrative burden
52
Annex 3 contains a completed checklist for identifying administrative requirements,
which shows that the proposal will not lead to any consequences that would exceed the usual
costs of real practice (i.e. current costs and payment for the services of classification societies).
Urgency
53
Despite the seemingly long deadline for nuclear FPU project commissioning (2029
and beyond), it seems advisable to immediately initiate work on the development of
non-mandatory safety guidelines for non-self-propelled nuclear FPUs. It should also be
remembered that the construction of one FPU takes about four years, and safety guidelines
should be taken into account starting from the design stage.

gold_evidence.context:
9
The requirements of SOLAS chapters II-1 and II-2 concerning the design of the oil
system and filters, inter alia, cover only the aspect related to fire hazard and, partially,
redundancy. For example, SOLAS regulation II-1/26.3 includes a requirement that means shall
be provided whereby normal operation of propulsion machinery can be sustained or restored
even though one of the essential auxiliaries becomes inoperative, including sources of
pressurized lubricating oil. However, the restoration time is not prescribed, which in practice
leads to the necessary stopping of the engine. The danger of a temporary loss of the main
engine's intended function and the associated potential loss of deck cargo are not reflected in
IMO instruments in any way. Although many classification societies have requirements in their
rules to ensure the possibility of cleaning and servicing fuel and oil filters without the need to
stop the engines, there is no universal requirement, resulting in many ships not being equipped
with such devices.

13
As a potential measure to respond to the situation described above, the
appropriateness of introducing an amendment to SOLAS regulation II-1/27 could be
considered in the future. Such an amendment could include the requirement that fuel and oil
systems of the main engine of ships intended for the carriage of deck cargo and containers on
the open deck should be designed to permit cleaning and servicing of fuel and oil filters without
the need to stop the systems.
Action requested of the Committee
14

The requirements of SOLAS chapters II-1 and II-2 concerning the design of the oil
system and filters, inter alia, cover only the aspect related to fire hazard and, partially,

systems of the main engine of ships intended for the carriage of deck cargo and containers on

question: 부유식 해상구조물에 설치하는 비상전원은 어떤 요건을 갖추어야 하며, 구체적으로 어느 장치들에 대해 최소 몇 시간 이상 급전이 가능해야 합니까?

clause: 401
조문 401절 401. 401. 개요
1. 적용
(1) 이 절의 규정은 시스템의 기능을 적절히 구현시키기 위해 소프트웨어에 의해 결정되는 컴퓨터기반시스템의 설계,
구성, 시운전 및 유지보수에 적용된다.
(2) 이 절의 규정은 선급기술규칙의 대상이 되는 제어, 경보, 감시, 안전 또는 내부통신 기능을 제공하는 시스템에 적용
된다.
2. 제외
(1) 법적 규정(statutory regulations)을 적용받는 컴퓨터기반시스템은 이 절의 요건에서 제외된다. 이러한 시스템의
예로는 해상인명안전협약(SOLAS) 제5장 및 제4장에서 요구하는 항해시스템 및 무선통신시스템, 선박의 적하지침
기기/복원성 컴퓨터가 있다.
(2) 적하지침기기/복원성 컴퓨터의 경우, IACS Rec. 48을 고려할 수 있다.

(다) IACS UR E27, 선내 시스템 및 장비의 사이버 복원력
(2) 참고 자료
이 절의 규정을 적용하기 위해서 컴퓨터기반시스템의 하드웨어 및 소프트웨어 개발용으로 다음의 표준이 사용될 수
있다.
(가) IEC 61508:2010, Functional safety of electrical/electronic/programmable electronic safety-related
systems
(나) ISO/IEC 12207:2017, Systems and software engineering – Software life cycle processes
(다) ISO 9001:2015, Quality Management Systems – Requirements
(라) ISO/IEC 90003:2018, Software engineering - Guidelines for the application of ISO 9001:2015 to
computer software

1. 일반 요구 사항
(1) 빌지 펌프는 공칭 전압의 87.5 % 즉, 12 V 장치의 경우 10.5 V, 24 V 장치의 경우 21 V에서 최고 전력소비를 야

다.
(2) 빌지 펌프와 빌지 펌프를 자동 운전하도록 전환시키는데 사용되는 장치는 ISO 8846의 요구 사항에 따라 발화 보
호되어 있어야 하고, ISO 10133의 전기적 요구 사항을 충족시켜야 한다.
(3) 빌지 펌프는 공칭 전압과 0 kPa, 10 kPa 및 20 kPa의 정압 즉, 0 m, 1 m 및 2 m의 출구 양정에서, 펌프 출구 바
깥지름과 같은 안지름을 갖는 내부가 매끄러운(smooth-bore) 호스로서 그 길이가 양정(lift)의 1.5배이고, 펌프 출
구에 부착된 호스에서 통과시킬 수 있는 수량은 liter/min 혹은 liter/hr에 의하여 정격이 정해져야 한다.
(가) 펌프의 정격과 용량은 펌프와 함께 제공된 설치 및 작동 매뉴얼에 명시되어야 한다.
(나) 펌프의 정격은 최대 배출 압력과 펌프가 작동 즉, 배수(discharge) 작용을 멈추었을 때의 양정(lift)을 포함해야
한다.

다.

아니 된다.

5. 트위스트 온(twist-on) 커넥터(와이어 너트)를 사용하여서는 아니 된다.

Local load distribution
The following local loads are to be applied for the calculation of hull girder shear and bending
moments:
a)
Ship structural steel weight distribution over the length of the cargo hold model (static
loads). The structural steel weight is to be calculated based on the FE model with a net
thickness of 0.5 tc deduction, as used in the cargo hold FE model.
b)
Weight of cargo and ballast (static loads).
c)
Static sea pressure, dynamic wave pressure and, where applicable, green sea load. For the
harbour/tank testing load cases, only static sea pressure needs to be applied.
d)
Dynamic cargo and ballast loads for seagoing load cases.
With the above local loads applied to the FE model, the FE nodal forces are obtained through FE
loading procedure. The 3D nodal forces will then be lumped to each longitudinal station to
generate the one dimension local load distribution. The longitudinal stations are located at
transverse bulkheads/frames and typical longitudinal FE model nodal locations in between the
frames according to the cargo hold model mesh size requirement. Any intermediate nodes created
for modelling structural details are not treated as the longitudinal stations for the purpose of local
load distribution. The nodal forces within half of forward and half of afterward of longitudinal
station spacing are lumped to that station. The lumping process will be done for vertical and
horizontal nodal forces separately to obtain the lumped vertical and horizontal local loads, fvi and
fℎi, at the longitudinal station i.

question: ABS 규정에 따라 SCR 시스템 설치 및 운용 시 엔진 성능에 미치는 영향과 관련하여 어떤 요구사항이 있습니까?
gold_answer:
- SCR 시스템은 엔진과 호환되어야 하며, 운전 중 과도한 배압이나 높은 온도로 인해 엔진 성능에 부정적인 영향을 주어서는 안 됩니다.

gold_evidence.context:
clause: 5
5.1.3
Visual and Audible Alarms
Alarms are to be both audible and visual, and are to be provided at the control stations, as listed in
Subsection 2/9. Alarms are to clearly identify the system and service of the faulted system or
components. Visual alarms are to be displayed in a distinguishable manner such that alarms for
similar components or systems are grouped together, and the colors representing a particular
function or condition remain uniform. Visual alarms are to flash when first activated. Audible
alarms associated with the machinery system or components are to be of a tone distinctive from
other alarms such as fire alarm, general alarm, gas detection, etc., and they are to be of sufficient
loudness to attract the attention of personnel on duty. For spaces of unusually high noise levels, a
beacon light or similar device, installed in a conspicuous place is to supplement any of the audible
alarms in such spaces. However, red light beacons are only to be used for fire alarms.
A fault in the visual alarm circuits is not to affect the operation of the audible alarm circuits.

clause: 5
5.1.4
Acknowledgement of Alarms
Alarms are to be acknowledged by manually changing the flashing display of the incoming alarm
to a steady display and by silencing the audible signal; the steady state light display is to remain
activated until the fault condition is rectified. Alarming of other faults that may occur during the
acknowledgement process is not to be suppressed by such action, and is to be alarmed and
displayed accordingly. The silencing of the audible alarm from a remote control and monitoring
center outside the machinery space(s) is not to lead automatically to the silencing of the original
alarm at the local centralized control and monitoring station(s) in or adjacent to the machinery
space(s) (if provided).
